::::{#exm-fubini-prob-fail}

#### When independence fails: a counterexample

Correctly applying @cor-fubini-joint requires the *actual* joint density $f_{X,Y}$
--- not the product of marginals $f_X(x)\,f_Y(y)$,
which is valid only when $X$ and $Y$ are independent.
Using the wrong joint density gives the wrong answer.

Let $X \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0, 1)$ and set $Y = X$
(so $X$ and $Y$ are perfectly correlated and **not** independent).

**True expectation:**

$$
\ba
\E{XY}
&= \E{X \cd X}
&& \text{(} Y = X \text{)}
\\&= \E{X^2}
&& \text{(} X \cd X = X^2 \text{)}
\\&= \int_0^1 x^2\,dx
&& \text{(LOTUS, with the uniform density } 1 \text{ on } [0, 1] \text{)}
\\&= \frac{1}{3}
&& \text{(integrate)}
\ea
$$

**Erroneously applying the product-measure formula:**

Note that Fubini--Tonelli's own conditions still hold here ($h(x,y) = xy$
is nonnegative and integrable), so the error is not a failure of
[Fubini--Tonelli](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/calculus-double-integrals.html#thm-fubini-tonelli) itself.
Rather, the error is using the *wrong measure*: the joint distribution
of $(X, X)$ is concentrated on the diagonal
$\{(x, x) : x \in [0, 1]\} \subset [0, 1]^2$,
which has Lebesgue measure zero in $\reals^2$.
The joint distribution is therefore **not** absolutely continuous with
respect to two-dimensional Lebesgue measure, so **no joint density
$f_{X,Y}$ on $[0, 1]^2$ exists**, which is the reference density
@cor-fubini-joint requires.

The following calculation is what someone would *erroneously* write
if they assumed independence and used $f_X(x)\,f_Y(y)$ as a "joint density"
--- a function that does not in fact correspond to the joint distribution of $(X, X)$.
The marginals $X \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$ and $Y \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$
do have densities

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_X &= f_Y \\
&= 1,
\end{aligned}
$$

but the *product* $f_X(x)\,f_Y(y) = 1$ on $[0, 1]^2$
is the density of an *independent* pair, not of $(X, X)$:

$$
\ba
\int_0^1\!\int_0^1 xy \cd f_X(x) \cd f_Y(y)\,dy\,dx
&= \int_0^1\!\int_0^1 xy\,dy\,dx
&& \text{(} f_X(x)\,f_Y(y) = 1 \text{ on } [0, 1]^2 \text{)}
\\&= \int_0^1 x\paren{\int_0^1 y\,dy}\,dx
&& \text{(factor } x \text{ out of the inner integral)}
\\&= \int_0^1 x \cd \frac{1}{2}\,dx
&& \text{(} \textstyle\int_0^1 y\,dy = \tfrac{1}{2} \text{)}
\\&= \frac{1}{4}
&& \text{(} \textstyle\int_0^1 \tfrac{x}{2}\,dx = \tfrac{1}{4} \text{)}
\ea
$$

This calculation recovers $\E{XY}$ for *independent* uniforms ($\tfrac{1}{4}$),
not $\E{XX}$ for the perfectly correlated pair ($\tfrac{1}{3}$).
The lesson is that @cor-fubini-joint requires the *actual* joint density $f_{X,Y}$.
For independent $(X, Y)$, this density factors as $f_X(x)\,f_Y(y)$;
for dependent $(X, Y)$, $f_{X,Y}$ need not factor
--- and for $(X, X)$, no joint density on $\reals^2$ exists at all,
so @cor-fubini-joint simply does not apply.

:::{#fig-fubini-prob-fail}

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| message: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| eval: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
set.seed(204)
n <- 400
x_dep <- runif(n)
y_dep <- x_dep
x_ind <- runif(n)
y_ind <- runif(n)

x_axis <- list(title = "Value of X", range = c(0, 1), scaleanchor = "y")
y_axis <- list(title = "Value of Y", range = c(0, 1))
legend_below <- list(orientation = "h", y = -0.2)
ind_marker <- list(size = 5, color = "#999999", opacity = 0.5)
dep_marker <- list(size = 6, color = "#b40426")

plotly::plot_ly() |>
  plotly::add_trace(
    type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
    x = x_ind, y = y_ind,
    name = "Assumed independent (X<sub>1</sub>, X<sub>2</sub>)",
    marker = ind_marker
  ) |>
  plotly::add_trace(
    type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
    x = x_dep, y = y_dep,
    name = "Actual (X, X) on diagonal",
    marker = dep_marker
  ) |>
  plotly::layout(xaxis = x_axis, yaxis = y_axis, legend = legend_below)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: !expr isFALSE(knitr::is_html_output())
#| results: asis

cat(
  "*(This scatter plot is interactive; see the HTML or slide version",
  "of this page to view it.)*"
)
```

Samples from the joint distribution of $(X, X)$ (red, on the diagonal)
versus an independent pair $(X_1, X_2)$ with the same marginals
(grey, scattered over $[0, 1]^2$).
The actual joint mass for $(X, X)$ is concentrated on a 1-dimensional diagonal
--- a set of Lebesgue measure zero in $\reals^2$ ---
so no joint density on $[0, 1]^2$ exists,
and the "$f_X(x)\,f_Y(y) = 1$" calculation integrates against the wrong measure
(the grey distribution).
